## Goal

We want a model that can generate all of the following outcomes:

$$
y_i=\mathbf{0},
\qquad
y_i\in \Delta^{K-1},
\qquad
y_{ik}=0,
\qquad
0<y_{ik}<1,
\qquad
y_{ik}=1.
$$

The aim is to build a coherent joint model where:

1. the row may be all zeros,
2. if the row is nonzero, only some components may be active,
3. if multiple components are active, mass is allocated with a Dirichlet distribution,
4. the hurdle, inclusion, and allocation processes all share the same latent index.

---

## Shared Latent Index

For observation $i$ and component $k$, define a shared latent score:

$$
\theta_{ik}=x_i^\top\beta_k.
$$

This score drives three related quantities:

$$
\mu_{ik}
=
\frac{\exp(\theta_{ik})}{\sum_{\ell=1}^K \exp(\theta_{i\ell})},
$$

$$
\rho_{ik}
=
\operatorname{logit}^{-1}\left(a_\rho \theta_{ik}-\tau_\rho\right),
$$

and a row-level nonzero probability

$$
\pi_i
=
\operatorname{logit}^{-1}
\left(
a_\pi\, h(\theta_i)-\tau_\pi
\right).
$$

Here:

- $\mu_{ik}$ is the allocation mean.
- $\rho_{ik}$ is the component-level inclusion probability.
- $\pi_i$ is the probability that observation $i$ has any positive mass.
- $a_\rho$ controls how strongly the latent score affects component inclusion.
- $\tau_\rho$ controls component-level sparsity.
- $a_\pi$ controls how strongly the latent scores affect the row-level hurdle.
- $\tau_\pi$ controls the probability of all-zero rows.

The function $h(\theta_i)$ summarizes the latent scores into a single row-level signal.

---

## Choosing the Row-Level Signal $h(\theta_i)$

A convenient choice is the log-sum-exp:

$$
h(\theta_i)
=
\log\sum_{k=1}^K \exp(\theta_{ik}).
$$

This quantity is high when the model assigns high latent intensity to at least one component.

Thus,

$$
\pi_i
=
\operatorname{logit}^{-1}
\left(
a_\pi \log\sum_{k=1}^K \exp(\theta_{ik})
-\tau_\pi
\right).
$$

### Intuition

The log-sum-exp behaves like a smooth maximum:

$$
\log\sum_k \exp(\theta_{ik})
\approx
\max_k \theta_{ik}.
$$

So the hurdle says:

> the row is likely to be nonzero when at least one component has high latent intensity.

This avoids using the observed active set $A_i$ to define the hurdle probability.

---

## Alternative Sampling-Effort Hurdle

If the data have a meaningful sample size or exposure $M_i$, use:

$$
\pi_i
=
1-
\prod_{k=1}^K
\left(1-\omega_{ik}\right)^{M_i},
$$

where

$$
\omega_{ik}
=
\operatorname{logit}^{-1}(a_\pi \theta_{ik}-\tau_\pi).
$$

This says:

> the row is nonzero if at least one latent component is detected after $M_i$ effective opportunities.

This is closer to the ZOID interpretation, but still keeps the latent index structure.

---

## Generative Model

The full generative model is:

$$
d_i\sim \operatorname{Bernoulli}(\pi_i).
$$

If

$$
d_i=0,
$$

then

$$
y_i=\mathbf{0}.
$$

If

$$
d_i=1,
$$

then draw a component active set:

$$
z_{ik}\sim \operatorname{Bernoulli}(\rho_{ik}),
$$

conditioned on

$$
\sum_{k=1}^K z_{ik}\ge 1.
$$

Let

$$
A_i=\{k:z_{ik}=1\}.
$$

Then:

- if $|A_i|=1$, the active component receives all mass;
- if $|A_i|\ge 2$, the positive components follow a Dirichlet distribution.

Specifically,

$$
y_{i,A_i}
\sim
\operatorname{Dirichlet}
\left(
\alpha_{i,A_i}
\right),
$$

where

$$
\alpha_{ik}
=
\phi
\frac{\mu_{ik}}{\sum_{\ell\in A_i}\mu_{i\ell}},
\qquad k\in A_i.
$$

Inactive components satisfy

$$
y_{ik}=0
\qquad
\text{for } k\notin A_i.
$$

---

## Full Likelihood

Define:

$$
A_i=\{k:y_{ik}>0\},
$$

and

$$
s_i=\sum_{k=1}^K y_{ik}.
$$

The likelihood has two cases.

### Case 1: all-zero row

If

$$
s_i=0,
$$

then

$$
\ell_i
=
\log(1-\pi_i).
$$

### Case 2: nonzero row

If

$$
s_i>0,
$$

define the normalized composition

$$
\tilde y_i=\frac{y_i}{s_i}.
$$

Then

$$
\ell_i
=
\log(\pi_i)
+
\log P(A_i\mid A_i\neq\varnothing)
+
\mathbf{1}(|A_i|\ge 2)
\log
\operatorname{Dirichlet}
\left(
\tilde y_{i,A_i}\mid \alpha_{i,A_i}
\right).
$$

The active-set probability is

$$
P(A_i\mid A_i\neq\varnothing)
=
\frac{
\prod_{k\in A_i}\rho_{ik}
\prod_{k\notin A_i}(1-\rho_{ik})
}{
1-\prod_{k=1}^K(1-\rho_{ik})
}.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\ell_i
=
\log(\pi_i)
+
\sum_{k\in A_i}\log\rho_{ik}
+
\sum_{k\notin A_i}\log(1-\rho_{ik})
-
\log
\left[
1-\prod_{k=1}^K(1-\rho_{ik})
\right]
+
\mathbf{1}(|A_i|\ge 2)
\log
\operatorname{Dirichlet}
\left(
\tilde y_{i,A_i}\mid \alpha_{i,A_i}
\right).
$$

The full sample log likelihood is

$$
\mathcal L
=
\sum_{i=1}^N \ell_i.
$$

---

## Component-Level Boundary Probabilities Conditional on Nonzero Row

Conditional on the row being nonzero, the component-level probabilities are:

$$
\Pr(y_{ik}=0\mid d_i=1)
=
\frac{
(1-\rho_{ik})
\left[
1-\prod_{m\ne k}(1-\rho_{im})
\right]
}{
1-\prod_{m=1}^K(1-\rho_{im})
},
$$

$$
\Pr(y_{ik}=1\mid d_i=1)
=
\frac{
\rho_{ik}\prod_{m\ne k}(1-\rho_{im})
}{
1-\prod_{m=1}^K(1-\rho_{im})
},
$$

and

$$
\Pr(0<y_{ik}<1\mid d_i=1)
=
\frac{
\rho_{ik}
\left[
1-\prod_{m\ne k}(1-\rho_{im})
\right]
}{
1-\prod_{m=1}^K(1-\rho_{im})
}.
$$

Unconditionally, these become:

$$
\Pr(y_{ik}=1)
=
\pi_i
\Pr(y_{ik}=1\mid d_i=1),
$$

$$
\Pr(0<y_{ik}<1)
=
\pi_i
\Pr(0<y_{ik}<1\mid d_i=1),
$$

and

$$
\Pr(y_{ik}=0)
=
(1-\pi_i)
+
\pi_i
\Pr(y_{ik}=0\mid d_i=1).
$$

This last expression reflects two ways for $y_{ik}=0$:

1. the entire row is zero;
2. the row is nonzero, but component $k$ is excluded.

---

## Ordered-Beta-Style Braces

The unconditional component-level distribution can be written as

$$
y_{ik}
\sim
\begin{cases}
0,
&
(1-\pi_i)
+
\pi_i
\dfrac{
(1-\rho_{ik})
\left[
1-\prod_{m\ne k}(1-\rho_{im})
\right]
}{
1-\prod_{m=1}^K(1-\rho_{im})
}
\$$18pt]

(0,1),
&
\pi_i
\dfrac{
\rho_{ik}
\left[
1-\prod_{m\ne k}(1-\rho_{im})
\right]
}{
1-\prod_{m=1}^K(1-\rho_{im})
}
\$$18pt]

1,
&
\pi_i
\dfrac{
\rho_{ik}\prod_{m\ne k}(1-\rho_{im})
}{
1-\prod_{m=1}^K(1-\rho_{im})
}.
\end{cases}
$$

The middle case is shorthand for the event that component $k$ is active along with at least one other component, in which case the positive subcomposition is Dirichlet-distributed.

---

## Interpretation of Parameters

| Parameter | Role | Interpretation |
|---|---|---|
| $\beta_k$ | shared latent index | affects hurdle, inclusion, and allocation |
| $\tau_\pi$ | row-level threshold | controls all-zero probability |
| $a_\pi$ | hurdle scale | controls how strongly latent intensity affects nonzero rows |
| $\tau_\rho$ | component threshold | controls sparsity among nonzero rows |
| $a_\rho$ | inclusion scale | controls how sharply components enter the active set |
| $\phi$ | Dirichlet precision | controls dispersion among active components |

---

## Why This Avoids Circularity

The model does **not** define the hurdle probability using the realized active set:

$$
A_i=\{k:y_{ik}>0\}.
$$

Instead, it defines the hurdle probability using the latent index:

$$
h(\theta_i)
=
\log\sum_{k=1}^K\exp(\theta_{ik}).
$$

This is known before $y_i$ is generated.

Thus the generative order is valid:

$$
\theta_i
\rightarrow
\pi_i
\rightarrow
d_i
\rightarrow
z_i
\rightarrow
A_i
\rightarrow
y_i.
$$

---

## Stan-Style Likelihood

```stan
real joint_hurdle_ordered_dirichlet_lpdf(vector y,
                                         vector theta,
                                         real phi,
                                         real tau_rho,
                                         real a_rho,
                                         real tau_pi,
                                         real a_pi) {
  int K = num_elements(y);
  real total = sum(y);

  // row-level hurdle using log-sum-exp signal
  real h = log_sum_exp(theta);
  real logit_pi = a_pi * h - tau_pi;

  if (total == 0) {
    return bernoulli_logit_lpmf(0 | logit_pi);
  } else {
    vector[K] y_norm = y / total;
    vector[K] rho;
    vector[K] mu = softmax(theta);
    real lp_A = 0;
    real log_empty = 0;
    int A_size = 0;
    array[K] int active;

    for (k in 1:K) {
      real eta_k = a_rho * theta[k] - tau_rho;
      real log_rho = -log1p_exp(-eta_k);
      real log1m_rho = -log1p_exp(eta_k);

      rho[k] = inv_logit(eta_k);
      log_empty += log1m_rho;

      if (y_norm[k] > 0) {
        A_size += 1;
        active[A_size] = k;
        lp_A += log_rho;
      } else {
        lp_A += log1m_rho;
      }
    }

    if (A_size == 0) {
      return negative_infinity();
    }

    lp_A -= log1m_exp(log_empty);

    if (A_size == 1) {
      return bernoulli_logit_lpmf(1 | logit_pi) + lp_A;
    } else {
      vector[A_size] y_A;
      vector[A_size] alpha_A;
      real mu_sum = 0;

      for (a in 1:A_size) {
        mu_sum += mu[active[a]];
      }

      for (a in 1:A_size) {
        int k = active[a];
        y_A[a] = y_norm[k];
        alpha_A[a] = phi * mu[k] / mu_sum;
      }

      return bernoulli_logit_lpmf(1 | logit_pi)
             + lp_A
             + dirichlet_lpdf(y_A | alpha_A);
    }
  }
}
```

---

## Relationship to Ordered Beta Regression

This model extends the ordered beta idea in two ways.

First, it preserves the ordered-beta-style triplet:

$$
0,\qquad (0,1),\qquad 1.
$$

Second, it adds an outer hurdle:

$$
\mathbf{0}
\qquad \text{versus} \qquad
\Delta^{K-1}.
$$

So the model is best understood as:

$$
\text{hurdle}
+
\text{ordered Dirichlet}
=
\text{zero-inflated ordered Dirichlet}.
$$

The shared latent index keeps the model parsimonious:

$$
\theta_{ik}=x_i^\top\beta_k
$$

drives:

- whether anything is present,
- which components are active,
- and how mass is allocated once active.

---

## Practical Recommendation

Use this joint hurdle ordered Dirichlet when:

- all-zero rows are meaningful,
- zeros within nonzero rows are also meaningful,
- ones are possible,
- and you want a single shared regression structure.

If all-zero rows are impossible by design, drop the hurdle and use the ordinary ordered Dirichlet.

If zeros are only sampling artifacts, a ZOID-style effective-sample-size model may be preferable.
